extracted.intended_audience: students and other writers revising academic essays or short papers
extracted.subtask_description: A revision checklist for revising academic essays, focusing on clarifying subject/audience/purpose, overall organization, paragraph-level coherence, sentence-level craft, and final proofreading/assignment checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject, audience, purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to clarify the paper's central message and its reader: What's the most important thing I want to say about my subject? Who am I writing this paper for? What would my reader want to know about the subject? What does my reader already know about it? Why do I think the subject is worth writing about? Will my reader think the paper was worth reading? What verb explains what I'm trying to do in this paper (tell a story, compare X and Y, describe Z)? Does my first paragraph answer questions 1-4? If not, why not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to ensure the thesis/purpose is clear and appropriate to the intended audience; explicitly identify the controlling verb (e.g., argue, describe, compare) and confirm the opening paragraph communicates subject, audience expectations, purpose, and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about the paper's overall structure: How many specific points do I make about my subject? Did I overlap or repeat any points? Did I leave my points out or add some that aren’t relevant to the main idea? How many paragraphs did I use to talk about each point? Why did I talk about them in this order? Should the order be changed? How did I get from one point to the next? What signposts did I give the reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the sequence of points supports the central idea, remove redundancies or irrelevant digressions, ensure proportional paragraphing for each point, and add clear transitions/signposting between ideas so readers can follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing (ask these questions of every paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph-level checks: What job is this paragraph supposed to do? How does it relate to the paragraph before and after it? What’s the topic idea? Will my reader have trouble finding it? How many sentences did it take to develop the topic idea? Can I substitute better examples, reasons, or details? How well does the paragraph hold together? How many levels of generality does it have? Are the sentences different lengths and types? Do I need transitions? When I read the paragraph out loud, did it flow smoothly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these to each paragraph to ensure each has a clear topic, appropriate development and unity, logical placement in the paper, varied sentence structure, necessary transitions, and smooth oral/read-aloud flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentences (ask these questions of every sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-level checks: Which sentences in my paper do I like the most? The least? Can my reader 'see' what I’m saying? What words could I substitute for people, things, this/that, aspect, etc.? Is this sentence 'fat'? Can I combine this sentence with another one? Can I add adjectives and adverbs or find a more lively verb?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these prompts to tighten prose: prefer concrete, specific wording; remove wordiness ('fat' sentences); combine or split sentences for clarity and rhythm; choose stronger verbs and selectively add modifiers to enliven expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Things to check last (final proofreading and reflection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final items before submitting: Did I check spelling and punctuation? What kinds of grammar or punctuation problems did I have in my last paper? How does my paper end? Did I keep the promises I made to my reader at the beginning of the paper? When I read the assignment again, did I miss anything? What do I like best about this paper? What do I need to work on in the next paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform line-level proofreading for mechanics and reflect on whether the conclusion fulfills the paper's initial promises; re-check the assignment requirements and note strengths/areas for growth for future revisions. — from A Rhetoric for Writing Teachers by Erika Lindemann
